knowledgePattern: Use turning heights and input domains to test transformed root counts

hints.title: Sketch the cubic before changing it
hints.body: Find the stationary points using f′(x)=0. The given graph crosses the x-axis three times, so its local maximum must be above the axis and its local minimum below it.
hints.recap: The heights of a cubic’s turning points help you count its roots.
hints.pitfall: Use the fact that the leading term is negative when sketching the two ends.
hints.pause: Mark <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> on your sketch and work out which sign <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math> must have.

recall.reminder: The heights of a cubic’s turning points help you count its roots.

hints.title: Turn I and II into horizontal lines
hints.body: Rearrange I and II so that the function equals a constant. On your cubic sketch, draw a horizontal line at each height.
hints.recap: The solutions of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>u</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></math> are the intersections with the line <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></math>.
hints.pitfall: For I, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></math> can be any real number; one convenient choice is not enough to prove “must”.
hints.pause: Test I for different heights. For II, check how many values of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> correspond to each value of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>u</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>x</mi></mrow></math>.

recall.reminder: Drawing a horizontal line on a graph lets you count solutions by counting intersections.

hints.title: Expand the expression in III
hints.body: Substitute −|x| into the formula for f, then subtract 3. Factor out a common power of x.
hints.recap: An equation with a product equal to zero can be solved by setting each factor equal to zero.
hints.pitfall: Check the sign of the cubic term carefully, and count distinct roots only once.
hints.pause: Solve the remaining factors using the sign of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math> you found, then decide which claims must hold.

recall.reminder: After factorising an equation, set each factor equal to zero to find its roots.

solution:
1. f′(x)=x(2k−3x), so the stationary inputs are 0 and 2k/3. Since f(0)=3>0 and the cubic has three distinct roots, 0 must be the local maximum and the other turning height must be negative. This requires k<0. If k≥0, the local minimum is at 0 with positive height, or the stationary inputs coincide, so three roots are impossible.

2. I is f(x)=a. An arbitrary horizontal level need not be between the turning heights: choosing a>3 gives only one intersection. Thus I is not guaranteed.

3. II is f(u)=5/2, where u=2−3x. This level lies strictly between the negative local minimum and the local maximum 3, giving three intersections. The linear input change is one-to-one, so it preserves their distinctness.

4. For III, f(−|x|)−3=|x|3+kx2=x2(|x|+k). Since k<0, its roots are 0,k,−k, all distinct. Hence II and III only: answer G.
